# SK6062 — The local collection is filled and never read

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A local collection is created, added to, and never enumerated, indexed, counted or handed anywhere — so the work that fills it is a feature that was started and abandoned.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Design |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

Both halves look correct in isolation, which is why review does not catch it: the declaration is ordinary, every `Add` is ordinary, and nothing is missing from any line. What is missing is a line. The compiler has nothing to say — a collection that is written to is used, as far as it is concerned — and every test over the method passes, because the method's observable behaviour is exactly what it would be with the collection deleted. ⚠ **The usual cause is a removed consumer**: the loop that read the list was deleted or moved and the loop that fills it was left behind, still paying for every element.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var failures = new List<string>();
foreach (var item in items) {
    if (!item.IsValid) {
        failures.Add(item.Name);
    }
}

return items.Count;   // nothing ever reads `failures`
```

Write:

```csharp
var failures = new List<string>();
foreach (var item in items) {
    if (!item.IsValid) {
        failures.Add(item.Name);
    }
}

return failures.Count == 0 ? items.Count : throw new ValidationException(failures);
```

## The ReSharper mapping

⚠ The export sets `resharper_collection_never_queried_local_highlighting` to `warning` and this rule defaults to `suggestion`, so importing the key raises it. The gap is deliberate: ReSharper answers the question across a whole solution and can see the reader this analyzer cannot, so its confidence is not available here. What ships is the slice one compilation can prove — a local, every one of whose references is a discarded write — and a slice that is narrower than the inspection it maps to does not inherit the inspection's severity.

## When it does not fire

**Locals only, and this is the whole reason the rule is decidable.** A field, a property or a parameter can be read by any member of the type and by anything holding the instance, so "nothing reads it" is not a claim a single compilation can make about one — which is the assembly boundary that closed [#114](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/114) and [#119](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/119), and the reason the `.Global` half of this concept is not here. A local's every reference is in one member and the analyzer can see all of them.

**Proved by exhaustion rather than by dataflow**, the argument `SK2083` uses for the mirror-image defect. Every reference to the local inside the declaring member must be the receiver of a mutating call whose result is discarded — an `Add`, `AddRange`, `Insert`, `Remove`, `RemoveAt`, `RemoveAll`, `Clear`, `Push`, `Enqueue`, `Sort`, `Reverse`, `TryAdd`, `TryTake` or `Enqueue` written as a statement — or the target of an indexer assignment. Anything else withdraws the finding without the analyzer having to decide what it does: an argument, a `return`, an assignment to anything, a `ref`, an interpolation, a capture, a `foreach` subject, a `.Count`, a LINQ call, a debugger-visible use. ⚠ **A discarded return value is required, not just tolerated**: `if (set.Remove(x))` reads the collection through the `bool`, and that is a use.

⚠ **`SK2083` and this rule are disjoint by construction rather than by filter.** `SK2083` reports a `foreach` over a collection nothing fills — it requires a read and forbids every write. This requires a write and forbids every read. No source can satisfy both, so the two can never report the same local.

⚠ **The scan runs over the whole enclosing member, not forward from the declaration**, so a lambda or local function declared above the local — which cannot capture it — and one declared below it — which holds a reference the scan sees — give the same answer. The result does not depend on statement order, which is what makes the exhaustion argument sound rather than merely usually right.

**Only collection types with a known empty constructor**, the same closed table `SK2083` resolves by symbol. A custom collection may have a `Add` that is the point of the call — writing to a logger, an accumulator with an observable side effect — and the rule has no way to know. Restricting to `List`, `HashSet`, `Dictionary`, `Queue`, `Stack` and their neighbours is what makes "nothing reads it" mean the collection is dead rather than that the analyzer cannot see the reader.

**Report-only, and not because a fix was hard to write.** Deleting the local means deleting every statement that writes to it, and those statements carry expressions — `failures.Add(Describe(item))` — whose evaluation may be the thing that mattered. More often the right edit is the opposite one: add the reader that was lost. The finding says the code is unfinished; it does not say in which direction, and an automated edit would have to guess.
